question.problem: At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}-xy=x+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-xy & =x+1 \\ {y}^{2}-xy-x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-xy-x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-xy-x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-xy-x)j \\  & =(2y-x)\,i+(y+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2y-x)\,i+(y+1)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2y-x & =0 \\ x & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=2y$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-(2y)y-(2y) & =1 \\ {y}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-2y-1 & =0 \\ -{y}^{2}-2y-1 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}+2y+1 & =0 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =0 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $y=-1$, we get $x=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,-1).$
